data.short_description: The year is 2033. Your name is Tex Murphy, Private Investigator in San Francisco.

reviews.review:
Tex Murphy: Martian Memorandum is a fascinating old-school detective adventure that captures a period when computer games were beginning to experiment seriously with multimedia storytelling. Developed by Access Software and currently published on Steam by Nightdive Studios and Atari, it follows private investigator Tex Murphy through a futuristic mystery filled with noir influences, science fiction, eccentric characters, humor, and increasingly dangerous discoveries. Its technology is obviously dated today, but the ambition behind its presentation and storytelling remains easy to appreciate.

Set in 2033, the story puts Tex in the familiar role of a struggling private investigator working in San Francisco. What begins as an investigation develops into a much broader mystery involving powerful individuals, corporate interests, Mars, and secrets with potentially enormous consequences. The narrative succeeds because it gradually expands its scope without abandoning the detective framework at its center. Tex spends much of the adventure pursuing leads, questioning people, searching locations, and attempting to understand how seemingly disconnected pieces of information relate to the case.

The point-and-click structure places greater emphasis on investigation and conversation than action. Exploring environments for clues and useful objects is fundamental to progression, while dialogue provides much of the information necessary to uncover new leads. This makes the player feel more like an investigator than simply someone moving between puzzles. Characters are especially important because questioning the right person about the correct subject can reveal information that pushes the case forward.

That investigative approach can also become one of the game's biggest challenges. Martian Memorandum belongs to an era when adventure games expected players to experiment extensively and tolerate being stuck. Important clues are not always obvious, and solutions can occasionally depend upon interactions that modern players may consider obscure. The inclusion of on-demand hint screens is therefore particularly welcome. It provides assistance without completely removing the satisfaction of solving the mystery independently.

Its mixture of detective noir and futuristic science fiction gives the adventure considerable personality. Tex resembles an old-fashioned private eye transported into a technologically advanced and somewhat dystopian world. Instead of treating that contrast with complete seriousness, the writing frequently embraces humor and eccentricity. The result is an atmosphere that can move between mystery, danger, comedy, cyberpunk, and science fiction without losing its identity.

The multimedia presentation is another defining feature. Animated talking characters, digitized speech, sound effects, music, and video-oriented sequences were highly ambitious elements for computer entertainment of its generation. They naturally appear primitive beside contemporary games, particularly in animation quality and visual resolution, but they provide important historical context. Martian Memorandum represents developers experimenting with ways to make adventure games feel more cinematic and character-driven long before full-motion video became a common selling point for PC titles.

Visually, the pixel graphics and digitized imagery have aged considerably, although they possess a distinctive retro appeal. Character portraits and environments communicate enough personality to support the detective atmosphere, while the unusual combination of noir imagery and futuristic locations gives the world a recognizable identity. Players interested in authentic early-PC aesthetics may actually find these limitations charming, whereas those expecting modern visual conveniences could struggle with the presentation.

The sound design deserves similar consideration. Digitized effects, spoken dialogue, and the musical score contribute greatly to the atmosphere even though their technical quality reflects their era. The talking characters are especially notable because they help conversations feel more personal than purely text-based exchanges. These elements also demonstrate how strongly the game was designed around the idea of multimedia entertainment rather than simply being a conventional graphical adventure.

Its strongest qualities are ultimately atmosphere, personality, and historical significance rather than mechanical sophistication. The detective framework remains engaging, the science-fiction mystery becomes increasingly interesting, and Tex himself provides enough personality to carry the investigation. The weaknesses largely come from age: occasionally confusing progression, archaic interface conventions, limited animation, dated audiovisual technology, and puzzle logic that can demand considerable patience.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently not officially confirmed with a Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification. The game does have Windows, macOS, and Linux versions and relies on DOSBox-era technology, so technically inclined Steam Deck users may be able to get it running, but it should not be treated as officially Deck-supported. Controller usability and configuration may also require additional adjustment compared with games specifically designed or verified for the handheld.

Martian Memorandum is consequently best recommended to players who enjoy classic point-and-click adventures, detective mysteries, retro computer games, or the history of multimedia storytelling. It is considerably harder to recommend to someone seeking modern conveniences and polished contemporary adventure mechanics. For players willing to accept its technological limitations, however, there is a creative and memorable detective story underneath them. It also represents an important stage in the development of Tex Murphy's distinctive blend of private-eye noir, comedy, cyberpunk, mystery, and cinematic experimentation.

Rating: 7/10
